reason: The paper introduces a benchmark-agnostic methodology for evaluating research agents' epistemic process from execution records, which is fundamentally an agent evaluation contribution, with a reward-hacking axis as a secondary aspect.
The paper proposes a monitoring method for agentic misalignment that complements and densifies chain-of-thought monitoring by tracking intent signals during the model's reasoning.

The paper introduces a safety benchmark for evaluating guardrail models on prompts, reasoning traces and responses of LRMs, which is primarily a safety evaluation benchmark contribution, with a secondary link to monitoring reasoning traces for unsafe content.
The paper's main contribution is an alignment evaluation of frontier models for dangerous unsanctioned behaviour (supply-chain attacks) in simulated cybersecurity tasks, which is a safety evaluation.
The paper proposes a trace-based failure attribution method for LLM coding agents performing vulnerability repair, localizing where silent security failures originate in the agent's workflow.

The paper studies whether models can learn steganographic (hidden) reasoning that evades chain-of-thought monitors, which falls squarely under evasion of CoT monitoring through encoded or obfuscated reasoning.

The main contribution is detecting and discovering reward hacking in frontier models via difference-of-means probes on internal activations, so the subject is reward hacking, with interpretability representations and action monitoring as secondary aspects.

The paper's main contribution is a method for assessing whether chain-of-thought engages and is causally grounded in the model's internal concepts, which is directly about CoT faithfulness; it uses shared SAEs and concept ablations as its tools.

The paper studies LLM overseers auditing other models' outputs with procedural traces, analyzing how their decision criteria and false-alarm behavior shift, which is a scalable-oversight and monitoring question.

The paper's main contribution is a conceptual criterion and recording convention for meaningful human oversight of delegated agentic (coding) systems, distinguishing accountable oversight from rubber-stamping.
The paper studies the reliability and invariance of chain-of-thought faithfulness detectors and proposes a hidden-state detector, so it falls squarely under CoT faithfulness methodology.
The paper studies whether LLMs deceptively conceal their own mistakes, measuring knowing concealment via chain-of-thought awareness, which is a core deception/honesty evaluation.
The main contribution is white-box probes for detecting deception and sabotage in LLM agents, including hidden goals, which falls squarely under deception detection in alignment and safety.

The paper analyses whether reasoning models' chains of thought do real computational work, combining circuit-complexity theory with chain-erasure experiments on reasoning models and GRPO checkpoints, which makes it primarily an analysis of reasoning models; it also bears on whether traces reflect the model's actual computation.
The paper introduces an attack (plan injection) that evades chain-of-thought monitors and studies monitorability failures, which is the core subject of CoT monitoring.

The paper detects post-rationalized (unfaithful) chains of thought where the model commits to a shortcut answer early, using internal confidence dynamics rather than the textual trace, which is the core concern of chain-of-thought faithfulness.
The paper analyzes how RLVR training changes the language of reasoning traces (language drift), with theory and experiments on its causes, while also drawing implications for CoT monitorability.
The paper adapts counterfactual tests to measure whether VLM chains of thought mention the visual evidence that actually influences predictions, which is directly about CoT faithfulness (omission).

The paper argues that security mechanisms relying on linguistic self-reports, including CoT monitoring and probing, cannot be fully sound, and proposes sandboxing via taint tracking, isolation and auditing as the main contribution to LLM and agent security.

The paper's main contribution is a causal measure (activation patching–based CoT Mediation Index) of whether models' internal computation actually depends on the emitted chain of thought, which is squarely about CoT faithfulness, with the layerwise causal patching method also placing it in circuits.

The main contribution is an inference-time plug-in that improves vision-language model reasoning on visual benchmarks, using SAE-like sparse dictionaries and activation injection as the mechanism rather than as the object of interpretability study.

The paper proposes an inherently interpretable hypergraph neural network architecture, which is graph learning outside language models (interpretability class is specific to language model internals).
The paper analyzes the geometry (Gromov hyperbolicity) of LLM hidden-state representations across layers, models, and domains, which is a study of representation geometry.

The main contribution is worst-case convergence analysis (lower and upper bounds) of the Muon/NorMuon optimizers, which is optimization theory, though it is motivated by and tested on LLM pretraining.
The paper develops adversarial observation attacks on model-based RL agents (DreamerV3) in control and game environments, which is RL robustness outside language models.
The main contribution is a multi-reward policy-gradient optimization method for LLM post-training, evaluated on math reasoning (correctness–cost) and on helpfulness–safety alignment.

The paper presents a mechanistic, causal analysis of the representations that matrix-valued memories learn on a group-composition task, showing that gradient descent recruits exactly the rank the task's algebra demands; since it is not specific to language models and fits none of the interpretability subclasses cleanly, the parent interpretability class is the best fit.

The paper studies retrieval-based in-context adaptation of vision-language-action robot policies, so its main subject is robot learning, with secondary relevance to retrieval augmentation and multimodal models.
The paper audits a sycophancy benchmark's prompt templates and identifies methodological confounds, making it chiefly a contribution to language model evaluation methodology.
The paper proposes an evaluation methodology for open-ended text generation, relating coherence and diversity metrics to human quality judgments, which fits language model evaluation.

The paper causally traces how Qwen2.5-7B implements number comparison via attention and MLP neurons, identifying and verifying a mechanism, while also analyzing representation geometry (linear vs. manifold).

The paper studies how LLMs internally organize mathematical computation by clustering activation-importance signatures, which is a representation-level interpretability analysis rather than a circuit-level causal analysis.

The paper introduces a mean-field kernel analysis of attention to model how a language model's representation geometry evolves across layers, which falls under interpretability of features and representations. It also tracks how the model diverges from its mean field over training around the onset of induction, so it belongs under training dynamics as well.
The core contribution is causal analysis via residual-stream and per-head activation patching of VLM failures, contrasting probe-decodable encoding with causal (in)activity.
The main contribution is a principled head-wise hybrid full/linear attention architecture design derived from head-level analysis, with length extrapolation as a key outcome.
The paper trains an explainer model to automatically generate natural-language explanations of SAE features, which is automated interpretability, with SAEs as the object being explained.

The paper introduces a diagnostic of representation similarity across layers of the residual stream, analysing representation geometry inside language models rather than proposing architectures or causal circuits.
The paper analyzes activation steering and the off-target interference it causes, which sits squarely in steering and model editing.
The paper's central subject is evaluation awareness, a safety concern listed under deception/sandbagging, studied via linear probes, verbalization, and steering across training stages.

The paper's main contribution is identifying internal representations (lens-based concept activations and residual-stream directions) that encode explore/exploit switching, with steering used to causally validate them.
The paper performs circuit discovery with causal ablations to identify the components responsible for animacy processing in LLMs, which is core circuits and causal analysis work.

The paper performs causal mechanistic analysis (activation patching, attention head identification) to explain how LLMs internally carry out propositional reasoning, which is circuit-level causal interpretability.
The paper introduces a method for finding causal abstraction alignments via interchange interventions, which is a core causal analysis technique for localizing mechanisms in neural networks.

The paper diagnoses and mitigates emergent misalignment arising from narrow fine-tuning, which the tree places under reward hacking and specification gaming (emergent misalignment from training), with a secondary mechanistic training-dynamics analysis.

The main contribution uses sparse autoencoder features, together with probes and causal interventions, to show that harmful-meme evidence is represented inside vision-language models but not routed to their outputs, which makes it an SAE-based interpretability study.

The paper analyzes how attention-head activity distributions change with serial task demand across many models, an interpretability study of internal routing that does not fit cleanly into one child (it uses attention activity analysis plus an ablation check rather than full circuit discovery).
The main contribution is a new contrastive sparse autoencoder variant (GI-SAE) used to find shared cross-language features in LLM representations, tested via feature swapping.

The paper's main contribution is showing that intervention-based faithfulness objectives used to evaluate circuits can misrank candidates, which makes it a methodological critique of interpretability evaluation applied to circuit discovery.

The paper studies how safety alignment degrades under ordinary fine-tuning, identifies an activation-space reversion direction, and uses it to build training objectives that preserve safety. That makes safety-motivated alignment training the best fit, with representation geometry as a secondary theme.

The paper proposes a measurement/audit criterion for correctly interpreting order-swap effects of activation-space interventions in language models, a methodological contribution to interpretability evaluation.

The paper studies subliminal learning, in which hidden teacher traits are transmitted through off-task distillation data, and how this transfer scales; it is a safety concern about unintended trait transmission and calls for trait-aware curation, and no child class (poisoning, deception, reward hacking) fits it precisely.

The paper's core contribution is a white-box framework reading latent knowledge from the residual stream with lens projections and probes. It shows a dissociation between linear decodability and causal control via ablation, which is centered on representations, with causal ablation and methodology as secondary aspects.
The paper presents a benchmark of image-borne prompt-injection-style attacks on agent skills, so its core contribution is agent security against injected instructions.

The main contribution is a vision-language video guardrail framework with fast-and-slow inference for content moderation, best placed under multimodal language models, with secondary ties to safety and test-time reasoning.
The paper introduces a black-box jailbreak attack that manipulates decoding via sampled text to bypass safety alignment.
The paper trains LLM auditors with RL to surface hidden or undesirable behaviors in target models, a scalable oversight and auditing contribution within alignment and safety.
The paper's main contribution is a backdoor/data-poisoning attack on unified autoregressive multimodal models, which falls under backdoors and poisoning in model security.

The paper's main contribution is about how safety monitors (input guards and activation probes) should be evaluated and improved, which falls under monitoring and control protocols; it also contributes safety evaluation methodology and robustness to rephrasing attacks.
The paper proposes a DPO-based preference optimization method that fuses multiple source models' probabilities, a contribution to preference training for general helpfulness.

The paper's main contribution is a formal framework and engine for agent harnesses (termination, spend bounds, independent verification gates), which is agent architecture/framework work, with secondary relevance to oversight and control of agent actions.
The paper proposes a multimodal jailbreak attack method (JMLLM) and a jailbreak dataset, squarely within jailbreaks and red-teaming.
The paper's main contribution is a defense against jailbreak attacks that unlearns harmful knowledge, which fits squarely under jailbreak robustness and defences.
The paper's central subject is evaluation awareness, which falls under deception/sandbagging/scheming in alignment and safety, studied via probing and mitigated via activation steering.

The paper frames filler-token hidden computation as a limit case for chain-of-thought monitoring and shows that it can be decoded from hidden states, arguing that monitorability extends beyond surface tokens; it uses interpretability tools such as logit lens and causal KV transplants to do so.

The paper studies how adversarial attacks degrade the calibration of guard-model safety classifiers, making jailbreak robustness of safety defences its central topic, with calibration and layer-wise representation analysis as supporting threads.

The paper's main safety concern is that distillation on unrelated data can covertly transfer backdoors and other hidden traits, which fits backdoors/poisoning under model security, with transferred hacking propensity also relating to reward hacking.

The paper's main contribution is a controlled benchmark for evaluating how tool-using agents report outcomes after tool failures, measuring false-success claims and fabricated details, which also ties it to hallucination.

The paper's main contribution is a reward-shaping method (PAR) designed specifically to mitigate reward hacking during RLHF, which fits the reward hacking and specification gaming class; it also contributes to RLHF preference training methodology.

The main contribution is an unsupervised deployment-time defence that flags unsafe or adversarial inputs as out-of-distribution, placing it under safety robustness and defences, with SAE-based local sparsity as the enabling technique.
The paper analyzes online RLHF versus offline preference optimization (e.g., DPO) for general LLM alignment, which falls under instruction tuning and preference training.
The main contribution is a GRPO-style RL policy optimization method with tree-based span-level credit assignment, applied to speech-aware LLMs.
The paper proposes a training method (on-policy distillation with stochastic teacher intervention) specifically designed for multi-turn agentic tasks, fitting agent-specific training methods.

The paper's main contribution is a training method specific to multi-turn language agents: on-policy distillation from off-the-shelf teachers, conditioned on a graph of teacher executions, evaluated on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and WebShop; it does not fit any single agent subclass, and the distillation aspect is the secondary tag.

The paper proposes a training intervention for on-policy distillation of reasoning from teacher to student on math benchmarks, which falls under reasoning post-training and distillation of reasoning rather than a specific child like RL from verifiable rewards.

The core contribution is a self-play RL post-training scheme with a self-verifier reward for improving VLM reasoning without labels, so reinforcement learning for reasoning fits best, with multimodal as a secondary class.

The main contribution is a modification of RLVR with ternary rewards, training reasoning models to abstain, which is RL for reasoning, and its aim of calibrated abstention also places it under hallucination and calibration.
The paper proposes a method to improve exploration and mitigate entropy collapse during RLVR training of LLMs for mathematical reasoning, using prefixes from weaker models.

The paper proposes a distillation method that generates student-compatible reasoning traces for SFT of small reasoning models, which is reasoning distillation under Reasoning and RL post-training, and none of its children (test-time compute, RL, analyses) fits better.

The paper analyzes what on-policy distillation of reasoning changes in student models, showing that it transfers compositional skill but not factual knowledge, which makes it an analysis of reasoning training.

The paper proposes a new advantage-estimation and credit-assignment method (CompPO), compared against GRPO and PPO, for RL post-training of LLMs on verifiable reasoning tasks; it uses attention statistics as a training signal rather than to explain the model, so it is not an interpretability paper.
The paper proposes a label-free test-time policy optimization objective combining grouped RL and on-policy self-distillation for mathematical reasoning, which is RL post-training for reasoning.

The paper proposes an on-policy distillation method for vision-language models acting as visual agents that interleave reasoning with image operations, making multimodal LMs the central subject, with agent training and reasoning distillation as secondary aspects.
The paper proposes a new RLVR training method mixing sparse off-policy interventions into on-policy rollouts for math and code reasoning, a policy optimization contribution for reasoning.
The paper proposes a GRPO-based RLVR objective augmented with gated on-policy teacher distillation for reasoning on math and code, a policy optimization method for reasoning.

The paper proposes a dynamic data selection and reweighting method for reinforcement fine-tuning that improves language-model reasoning, so it is a policy-optimization contribution to RL for reasoning.

The paper studies on-policy self-distillation objectives as reasoning post-training methods (attractive, repulsive, contrastive) and analyzes their effects on reasoning behavior and length. This spans RL-style post-training and distillation of reasoning, so it is placed in the parent class, with its analyses of response length and thinking-mode switches also fitting reasoning-analyses.
The paper proposes a GRPO-based policy optimization method with token-level credit assignment from verified evidence for reasoning and tool-use tasks, squarely RL from verifiable rewards.

The core contribution is RL with verifiable rewards (evolution-aware RL on code execution signals) to train self-reflection/refinement meta-skills, with inference-time evolutionary search as a secondary component.

The main contribution is a research-level math dataset plus distilled teacher reasoning trajectories used to train models for mathematical reasoning, which fits reasoning post-training and distillation of reasoning; the multi-agent pipeline is only the curation tool.
The paper's main contribution is a prompt-injection and memory-poisoning attack on LLM agents, which is agent security under prompt injection and model security.
The main contribution is a new executable environment and benchmark for evaluating and RL-training LLM agents on long-horizon embodied planning, which fits agent benchmarks and environments.
The paper proposes a decentralized coordination protocol for multiple embodied LLM agents exchanging executable commitments, which is centrally about multi-agent LLM cooperation.
The paper presents a framework for selecting and adapting tool APIs for web agents operating browsers, evaluated on WebArena, which is squarely web/computer-use agents.
The paper studies how disclosed model-identity labels cause factionalism and degrade cooperation among interacting LLM agents, a core multi-agent systems question.

The paper proposes synthetic edge-case task generation to train and optimize the harnesses of tool-calling agents, so it is an agent-specific training method that fits the general agents class rather than any single child.
The paper presents a test-time memory and retrieval framework, built from historical pull requests, that improves LLM coding agents on SWE-Bench-style repository tasks.
The paper contributes a statistically valid evaluation protocol for comparing agent workflows on benchmarks like τ-bench, which is agent evaluation methodology.
The main contribution is a benchmark with trace-grounded checks and a risk-preserving subset selector for evaluating memory-related risks in long-horizon LLM agents, which is agent evaluation.
The paper trains memory-management policies for long-horizon LLM agents with a hindsight process reward model, an agent-specific training method centered on agent memory.
The paper's main contribution is a long-horizon interactive benchmark for evaluating agentic vision-language models, which fits agent benchmarks and evaluation, with a secondary multimodal focus.

The paper studies emergent failure modes such as collusion and conformity that arise when multiple LLM agents interact, which makes multi-agent systems its core subject; because it frames these behaviours as safety risks, it also fits safety evaluations.

The paper's main contribution is a training method specific to recursive language-model agents (task decomposition, delegation and self-generated rubrics as rewards), which falls under the agents class rather than any of its narrower subclasses; it also uses reward-model-style RL post-training, so rl-for-reasoning is listed as a secondary class.

The paper studies language models as outcome predictors (world models) inside AI research agents' propose-implement-evaluate loops, including multi-round Autoresearch, making it chiefly about agent capabilities and planning rather than any narrower agent subtype.

The main contribution is an agentic retriever model trained via SFT and GSPO to return ranked evidence for downstream generation, which is fundamentally retrieval-augmented generation, with agentic multi-step search and a Russian benchmark as secondary aspects.
The main contribution is a benchmark/evaluation framework with trajectory-level privacy metrics for realistic LLM agent workflows, with runtime auditing touching on agent security.

The paper proposes a method for automatically optimizing agent harnesses (architecture/framework code coordinating context, state, and tool calls), which is a general agent-architecture contribution not specific to coding, computer use, multi-agent, or evaluation subfields.

The paper proposes a hierarchical decentralized framework for coordinating many LLM-based agents, which is a multi-agent systems contribution; its differential-privacy and secure-aggregation knowledge sharing also places it in federated and privacy-preserving learning.

The paper trains language-model textual world models that predict environment evolution for agents in text environments like ScienceWorld and Jericho, using structured reasoning with intermediate predictive rewards; this fits agents best, with a secondary reasoning/RL component.

The paper proposes a training-free decoding/reranking method that makes vision-language-action robot policies safer on embodied manipulation and navigation tasks, which falls under robot learning and embodied AI.
The paper proposes a post-training quantization method for LLMs, which falls squarely under inference efficiency (quantization).

The main contribution is compressing documents into fixed-size transferable latent states that replace long raw-text context for frozen reader LLMs, a context-compression and memory method, with retrieval-augmented generation as the key application.

The paper proposes a memory-efficient low-rank gradient projection optimizer improvement (rank allocation and gradient decomposition) to speed LLM pretraining, which is training efficiency and optimizers at scale.
The main contribution is a training-free KV cache eviction method for bounded-memory inference in hybrid video-language models, which is a KV-cache efficiency technique.
The paper proposes a KV-cache-aware request scheduling algorithm for LLM serving in vLLM, which is an inference serving efficiency contribution.

The paper proposes a training-free model-merging method that composes thinking and non-thinking checkpoints to cut reasoning-token overhead (overthinking) while keeping accuracy, so it belongs under reasoning models and their efficiency, alongside analysis of what reasoning training changes in the weights.
The paper proposes a training-free KV-cache eviction method to reduce inference memory, which falls squarely under KV-cache inference efficiency.

The paper proposes a training-free parallel decoding method that raises decoding throughput in masked diffusion language models while maintaining accuracy, which is an inference-efficiency contribution.
The paper proposes a batch-aware expert selection method with custom kernels to speed up MoE decoding during serving, which is an inference-efficiency contribution.

The paper studies precomputed KV-cache memory and trained cache compressions as a substitute for re-reading context, which is a long-context memory and context-compression topic, with additional relevance to KV-cache inference efficiency.
The paper proposes a structured expert pruning method for MoE language models to reduce deployment memory, which is an inference-efficiency (pruning) contribution.
The main contribution is a latent action mechanism unifying fast-weight memory recall and latent reasoning to address long-context reasoning, best fitting long context and memory mechanisms.

The main contribution is an FP4 quantization (quantization-aware training plus KV-cache quantization) method that makes RL rollouts of MoE models efficient, which is primarily a quantization/efficiency contribution.

The main contribution is a new transformer architecture and scaling paradigm (a two-tower MoE decoder with KV-invariant expansion via upcycling), with secondary gains in inference and training efficiency.
The paper proposes a post-training quantization method for compressing LLMs, which falls squarely under inference efficiency (quantization).

The paper's main contribution is a distributed training system (ring-based MoE dispatch and recomputation) that improves memory efficiency and throughput, which falls under training efficiency and systems.

The paper proposes a training framework for masked diffusion language models, an alternative to standard autoregressive transformer modelling, aimed at aligning training with the inference trajectory; it also cuts the number of function evaluations needed at inference.
The paper proposes a speculative decoding framework that accelerates LLM inference, which falls squarely under inference efficiency.

The paper co-designs hardware mapping, optimizer and converters so that Transformer training scales on analog in-memory computing hardware, which makes it primarily a training efficiency and systems contribution.
The paper proposes a new tokenizer training method and encoding algorithm, which falls under tokenization in the pretraining, data and scaling class.
The paper's main contribution is an optimization convergence analysis for Riemannian minimax methods applied to distributionally robust optimization, which is not specific to language models.
The paper proposes a heterogeneous graph message-passing method with meta-path attention for relational database learning, which is primarily graph learning, with relevance to tabular data.
The paper's main contribution is a hierarchical graph neural network architecture (Kron-reduced graph communication) for power-flow prediction, a graph learning method applied to power grids.
The paper proposes a prompt initialization method for pre-trained graph neural networks on node and graph classification, which is graph learning rather than language modeling.

The paper develops a JEPA-style predictive representation learning framework for modeling parametric PDE dynamics, which is a scientific machine learning application rather than language model research.
The paper develops a flow-matching method for single-cell trajectory inference from Markov transition graphs, an application of generative modeling to biology.
The paper applies supervised ML classifiers to tabular clinical features for stroke prediction, a medical application of machine learning.
The paper presents a medical application: an eye-tracking representation learning network for autism screening, which falls under AI for health rather than language models.
The main contribution is a federated learning framework for graph clustering across clients, which fits federated learning first and also graph learning.
The paper applies machine learning to a medical problem, building a prescriptive clinical support tool for heart valve selection, so it falls under AI for science and health.
The paper develops theory and convergence guarantees for Q-learning with linear function approximation, which is RL theory outside language-model post-training.
The paper proposes a chunking framework, built on cell role annotation, that prepares spreadsheets for LLM retrieval-augmented generation, so its main contribution is to RAG.
The paper's main contribution is a diffusion model for synthetic tabular data generation, which falls under tabular data modeling; LLMs are only used as an auxiliary tool for prior extraction.

The paper applies classical ML (gradient boosting) to predict retransmissions from recent HARQ feedback history for 5G link adaptation, which fits best as sequential/tabular prediction outside language models, since no class covers wireless networking directly.
This is a medical physics application that uses a pretrained CT foundation model with registration to forecast anatomy for adaptive proton therapy, so it falls under AI for health.
The paper presents a medical imaging segmentation method for PET/CT lesions, which is an AI application to health rather than language-model research.

The paper presents an unsupervised deep clustering method that reorganizes pretrained text and image embeddings, which is general ML research not about language models themselves and fits no specific child class well.

The paper applies instruction-tuned LLMs to argument mining, an information-extraction-style language task, so its main contribution is a task application rather than general instruction-tuning research.
The paper proposes a learnable noise sampling distribution for diffusion models applied to image super-resolution, a diffusion-based image generation contribution.

The paper is a combinatorial optimization/algorithmic study of strong independent sets in hypergraphs (reductions, bounds, greedy certificates), best fitting classical AI/constraint solving and symbolic algorithms rather than any language-model topic, with deduplication only as motivation.

The paper develops a constrained imitation-learning training scheme for neural-network control policies, evaluated on autonomous racing, which fits robot learning and control rather than language models; its convergence analysis as inexact projected gradient descent is a secondary optimization-theory contribution.

The paper's main contribution is an evaluation and reporting method for an operational Earth-observation (Sentinel-1 SAR) rare-event classifier, which is an applied-science ML application rather than a language-model topic.
The paper's core contribution is a diffusion Schrödinger bridge generative model for audio (speech enhancement), which fits generative models for audio rather than language models.
The paper applies protein generative model priors to cryo-EM structure determination, a structural biology application of machine learning.

The paper's core is a real-time multilingual lip-synchronization video generation system with pipeline parallelism and inference optimizations, which fits audio/video generation more than language-model research.
The paper's main contribution is a self-supervised monocular depth/distance and ego-motion estimation method for fisheye cameras, which is a 3D computer vision task, applied to autonomous driving.

The paper extends a symbolic music processing library to support expression text and introduces generative music tasks, so it fits best under generative models for audio/music rather than language models.
The paper proposes CNN and GAN super-resolution models and a dataset for downscaling satellite cloud masks, a remote-sensing computer vision task with Earth-science applications.
The paper proves tight lower bounds on oracle complexity for stochastic nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization, which is optimization theory not specific to language models.
A general survey of machine learning under missing, imbalanced, weakly labelled and shifted data, not focused on language models and spanning several ML subareas, so the parent class fits best.
The paper proposes a robust SGD optimization method with convergence proofs for finite-sum problems with corrupted components, unrelated to language models.

The paper benchmarks the memory use of stream classifiers (Hoeffding trees, adaptive ensembles) on data streams with concept drift, which is non-LM machine learning closest to the time-series and tabular data class.

The main contribution is synthetic time-series data generation for manufacturing, using fine-tuned LLMs with RAG as the generator, which is evaluated against ARIMA and LSTM baselines and on downstream anomaly detection.
The paper gives a theoretical analysis of a boosting algorithm for multicalibration, which is learning theory not specific to language models.
The paper applies LLMs to lossy text compression via deletion and reconstruction, an application of language models to a text-processing task, with ties to context compression.
The paper applies learning-based system identification to recover interaction laws in physical interacting particle systems, a scientific application outside language models.
The paper applies RL agents to correct biases in a numerical weather prediction model, an AI-for-science application to atmospheric physics.
The paper is a theoretical study of neural network approximation, establishing minimal neuron counts and bit complexity, so it falls under learning theory rather than any language-model topic.
The paper proposes a peer selection method for decentralised federated learning, with optimal-stopping theory and guarantees, which places it squarely in federated learning.
The paper proposes a robust cooperative multi-agent RL method for noisy observations (StarCraft II), unrelated to language models, which places it under reinforcement learning.
The paper proposes a Bayesian nonrigid registration method aimed at spatial transcriptomics data, so it is mainly a machine-learning application to biology rather than language-model work.
The paper's core contribution is a diffusion-based generator for synthetic tabular data, which falls under tabular models, with causal-effect preservation as a secondary causal-inference theme.
The paper evaluates and fine-tunes time-series foundation models for covariate-aware counterfactual forecasting and system identification, so it belongs under time series rather than language models.

The paper introduces a text-and-audio benchmark and evaluates multimodal (audio-language) models on detecting vocal confidence and evasion, making multimodal language models the central subject, with a financial domain application.
The paper gives a theoretical smoothed analysis of A* search with inconsistent heuristics, a classical search and planning topic.
The paper proposes a Thompson sampling algorithm for non-stationary contextual bandits, which is a bandit/RL algorithm unrelated to language models.
The paper fine-tunes a flow-matching diffusion image model (FLUX.1 Kontext) with LoRA for controllable image editing of lighting, which is generative media modeling.

The paper is a formal-methods and automata-theory result: it proves type-checking decidable for pattern-based tree transformations by reduction to the emptiness problem of alternating tree automata, which fits symbolic reasoning and logic best.

The paper's main contribution is a causal discovery method for orienting edges beyond the Markov equivalence class, using LLM-assigned tags only as auxiliary input, so it belongs under probabilistic and causal inference.

The paper studies LLM-synthesized code world models used by planners, characterizing certification limits and errors beyond the reachable set and how to mitigate them, which fits language-model agents with world models and planning better than any narrower agent subclass.
A position paper on reformulating offline RL objectives toward adaptive policy priors, which is RL research outside language-model post-training.
The paper develops interpretable structural node descriptors for node classification on graphs, which is graph learning outside language models, with a drug-target application on protein networks.

The paper is a data analysis of coverage and spatial bias, i.e. inequalities in media attention, in German news reporting on landslides, which best matches social bias and impact studies rather than any language-model or ML method contribution.

The paper's main contribution concerns cross-lingual transfer to 13 non-English languages for sequential sentence classification, including a new multilingual dataset and an analysis of which source-target similarities predict transfer success.

The paper learns sparse, interpretable feedback control policies for nonlinear dynamical systems via differentiable predictive control, a control/learning-for-control topic closest to robotics and control, with no language-model content.

The paper evaluates the validity of LLM annotations in an education domain application (diagnosing student errors in tutoring dialogue), showing that cross-model consensus does not imply validity, which places it among domain applications of language models with an evaluation-methodology angle.

The paper proposes a kernel-based decoder that adapts frozen multimodal large language model representations to downstream prediction tasks, so its main subject is the adaptation of multimodal language models.

The paper studies the geometry and certified reconstruction of full conformal prediction regions, a statistical uncertainty-quantification topic outside language models that best fits probabilistic inference.
The paper studies latent world models for forecasting multichannel CNC sensor time series and their transfer across machines, which is primarily time-series forecasting outside language models.

The paper is a computational social choice and formal argumentation study, covering voting axioms, complexity results and Lean formalisation, which fits best under classical AI and knowledge representation.
The paper gives a convergence analysis of TD learning with target networks via a stochastic contraction framework, which is RL theory outside language-model post-training.

The paper applies survival/time-to-event models to tabular e-commerce repurchase data for recommendation. No class covers recommender systems, and the tabular, time-to-event prediction work fits time-series and tabular data most closely.
The paper proposes JEPA world models for communication-aware remote robot control and navigation, which is robot learning outside language models.

The paper's main contribution is a black-box optimization method that uses an unconditional generative sampler as a corruption-refinement operator, which makes it optimization research outside language models; the closest fit is learning theory and optimization, with a secondary fit to generative models.
The paper's main contribution is a medical imaging application: a new real-world ultra-low-dose lung CT dataset together with a denoising method for it, which places it in AI for health.

The paper studies neural surrogates for an expensive solver in a general-relativistic radiation-hydrodynamics code, which is a machine-learning application to physics simulation rather than language model research.
The paper proposes a communication-efficient federated multi-objective optimization method with convergence analysis, centrally a federated learning contribution.

The paper applies input-attribution methods to EEG foundation models for clinical and neuroscientific validation. It is a health/neuroscience application of machine learning rather than interpretability of language models' internal mechanisms.
The paper's main contribution is a multi-objective RL locomotion policy for a quadrupedal robot that transports unsecured payloads, with sim-to-real transfer, which is robot learning.
